candidates.summary: Google DeepMind said human-guided AI agents uncovered two major weaknesses in legacy 1024-bit RSA cryptosystems (signature padding forgery shortcuts and ~30× cheaper batch factoring per additional same-size key), while stating modern 2048-bit and larger RSA remain safe from these specific exploits.
facts: @GoogleDeepMind / @pushmeet (2026-11-06): research framed as AI agents accelerating cryptanalysis stress-tests; work led by Dj Dvijotham and Abhradeep Thakurta with Nadia Heninger (UC San Diego/Inria) and Emmanuel Thomé (Inria).

Signature-padding result: once an attacker controls roughly half or more of the signed block, padding adds no forgery protection; sandboxed reproduction on an already-solved 1024-bit benchmark key used 3.5× less CPU than prior, at <1/1000th the compute to break the key itself. For short 32-byte fingerprints they report a new algorithm ~1,600× better than prior best on 1024-bit (theoretical estimates).
Batch factoring: agents found a new algorithm with better asymptotic complexity, cutting average cost of factoring each additional 1024-bit key in a batch by about 30× vs prior batch NFS methods.
DeepMind: modern protocols almost universally use 2048-bit+ keys and remain secure; papers posted at storage.googleapis.com/deepmind-media/papers/ (Faster Affine Root… and Fan Factories / Batch NFS).

candidates.summary: a16z's Asaf Ezra and Steph Zhang published 'Defense in Depth, Rebuilt for Machine Speed,' arguing AI-cheap exploits mean the fix is not faster patching but products that make patching unnecessary, and listing six cybersecurity company openings from live fixes to long-tail platforms.
facts: a16z.news (2026-11-06) follow-up to their exploit-was-the-bottleneck thesis: cites Verizon 2026 median full remediation 43 days / only 26% of known-exploited vulns fully remediated; Veracode 2025 average flaw remediation 252 days (up from 171 five years earlier).

October PHP critical bugs leaked before fix; exploit attempts began four days before public disclosure; ~2.6–4.4M installs outside CDN/hosting umbrellas stayed exposed. Anthropic reportedly had an unreleased model produce a remote no-login Linux kernel LPE in under an hour for a bug still unfixed in two major server distros.

Six openings: (1) live fixes then code fixes, (2) AI first-responder SOC without hand-written rules, (3) per-request access for people and agents with minute-lived credentials, (4) proven recovery / backup posture with insurer-grade restore records, (5) install gateway sandboxing packages/extensions/agent tools, (6) managed long-tail security for utilities/clinics lacking security teams.
@a16z summary post: 'So the question isn't how to patch faster. It's how to stop needing to.'

candidates.summary: LangChain shipped async subagents for Deep Agents: an orchestrator stays responsive to the user while background subagents run long tasks, with start/check/update/cancel/list tools and interrupt vs enqueue steering; available in Python, JavaScript, and Managed Deep Agents.
facts: LangChain blog 'Agents Are Going Async' (Sydney Runkle & Thushanth Bengre, 2026-11-05): ReAct loops block on long tool calls; async pattern mirrors Claude Code background subagents, OpenAI dots workers, and DeepSeek Harness router+workers.

Tools: start_async_task, check_async_task, update_async_task, cancel_async_task, list_async_tasks. update_strategy 'interrupt' (default) restarts with new instruction; 'enqueue' waits until current run finishes.

Notifications: unfinished tasks listed in orchestrator system prompt; busy orchestrator polls before each model call; idle orchestrator woken by finished subagent; approvals left alone until user answers. Task notifications marked beta.
@hwchase17 (2026-11-06): week's ship also includes browser-use tuning in MDA (7 toolsets; Stagehand won), LangSmith BYOC on AWS/Azure/GCP, and Interrupt conference back March 24–25 in SF.

candidates.summary: Alexander Yue argued lossy summary handoffs make subagents a top failure mode, measured 'checkpoint' session forks vs classic subagents on a 137k-token Opus 5.5 session, and concluded most work is better done serially with retrieval or as fresh parallel sessions rather than partial delegation.
facts: @Alezander9 (2026-11-06 01:35 UTC): classic pattern = main agent summarizes → subagent assumes from summary → returns another summary; same flaw as compaction.
Checkpoint idea: fork the session so the worker shares identical cached prefix with the main agent; returning work keeps main-agent cache warm.

Measured 137k-token Opus 5.5 session: solo main 67s / $0.38 / +8–17k context; checkpoint 117s / $0.68 / +2k; classic subagent 123s / $0.57 / +4–5k. Concluded avoiding large input mattered more than cache, and 'I do not think there is a place for subagent delegation at all' between a pure orchestrator and a long-running retrievable agent.
Midday X news cluster 'Developers Question Subagent Delegation' cited this thread alongside Claude Code cheaper background-status updates.

Verbatim via Simon: 'The products aren't good enough to sell people on the costs… You cannot tell people that you have to listen to the whine of a data center in their backyard for AI overviews and some of the most hilarious deep fake slop in history.'

candidates.summary: arXiv 2611.08341 proposes evaluating compressed AI-agent memory with both local nearest-neighbor fidelity and global far-apart structure, arguing agents that consolidate/delete/compare memories need the global end, not only local neighbor survival after compression.
facts: Submitted 2026-11-05 (cs.AI agents filter): 'Enhancing Local and Global Structure in Compressed AI Agent Memory.'

Abstract: compression often accepted when nearest neighbors survive, but consolidate/delete/compare depend on which items lie far apart; evaluate local fidelity L at 10 neighbors and global fidelity G at 30–50% of memory.
At 96 bytes per passage, rescored binary codes reach L of 0.97 (abstract continues with further compression/fidelity tradeoffs).
